Main.sentence: Margaret Hilda Thatcher, Baroness Thatcher [nb 2] ( née Roberts ; 13 October 1925 – 8 April 2013), was a British stateswoman who served as ___E:Prime Minister of the United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom)___ from 1979 to 1990 and ___E:Leader of the Conservative Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Conservative_Party_(UK))___ from 1975 to 1990. She was the ___E:longest-serving British prime minister U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_prime_ministers_of_the_United_Kingdom_by_length_of_tenure)___ of the 20th century and the first woman to hold the position.
As prime minister, she implemented policies that came to be known as ___E:Thatcherism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thatcherism)___ .
A Soviet journalist dubbed her the " Iron Lady ", a nickname that became associated with her uncompromising politics and ___E:leadership style U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_style)___ .

Thatcher studied chemistry at ___E:Somerville College, Oxford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerville_College,_Oxford)___ , and worked briefly as a ___E:research chemist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_chemist)___ before becoming a ___E:barrister U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barristers_in_England_and_Wales)___ .

She was ___E:elected Member of Parliament U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_MPs_elected_in_the_1959_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ for ___E:Finchley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finchley_(UK_Parliament_constituency))___ in ___E:1959 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1959_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ . ___E:Edward Heath U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Heath)___ appointed her ___E:secretary of state for education and science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_state_for_education_and_science)___ in his ___E:1970–1974 government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heath_ministry)___ .

In 1975, she defeated Heath in the ___E:Conservative Party leadership election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_Conservative_Party_leadership_election)___ to become ___E:leader of the opposition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_(United_Kingdom))___ , the first woman to lead a major political party in the UK.

On becoming prime minister after winning the ___E:1979 general election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ , Thatcher introduced a series of economic policies intended to reverse high inflation and Britain's struggles in the wake of the ___E:Winter of Discontent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_of_Discontent)___ and ___E:an oncoming recession U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_1980s_recession)___ . [nb 3] Her political philosophy and economic policies emphasised ___E:greater individual liberty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian_conservatism)___ , the privatisation of ___E:state-owned companies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_companies)___ , and reducing the power and influence of ___E:trade unions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_unions_in_the_United_Kingdom)___ .
Her popularity in her first years in office waned amid the recession and rising unemployment.

Victory in the 1982 ___E:Falklands War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falklands_War)___ and the recovering economy brought a resurgence of support, resulting in her ___E:landslide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landslide_victory)___ re-election in ___E:1983 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ .

She survived an assassination attempt by the ___E:Provisional IRA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_IRA)___ in the 1984 ___E:Brighton hotel bombing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton_hotel_bombing)___ and achieved a political victory against the ___E:National Union of Mineworkers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Union_of_Mineworkers_(Great_Britain))___ in the ___E:1984–85 miners' strike U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984%E2%80%9385_miners%27_strike)___ .

In 1986, Thatcher oversaw the ___E:deregulation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deregulation)___ of UK ___E:financial markets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_market)___ , leading to ___E:an economic boom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawson_Boom)___ , in what came to be known as the ___E:Big Bang U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_(financial_markets))___ .

Thatcher was re-elected for a third term with another landslide in ___E:1987 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ , but her subsequent support for the ___E:Community Charge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_Charge)___ (also known as the "poll tax") was widely unpopular, and her increasingly ___E:Eurosceptic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euroscepticism_in_the_United_Kingdom)___ views on the ___E:European Community U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Community)___ were not shared by others in her cabinet.

She resigned as prime minister and party leader in 1990, after a ___E:challenge was launched to her leadership U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Conservative_Party_leadership_election)___ , and was succeeded by ___E:John Major U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Major)___ , her ___E:chancellor of the Exchequer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_of_the_Exchequer)___ . [nb 4] After retiring from the ___E:Commons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom)___ in 1992, she was given a ___E:life peerage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_peer)___ as Baroness Thatcher (of ___E:Kesteven U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kesteven)___ in the ___E:County of Lincolnshire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Lincolnshire)___ ) which entitled her to sit in the ___E:House of Lords U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords)___ .

In 2013, she ___E:died of a stroke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_funeral_of_Margaret_Thatcher)___ at ___E:the Ritz Hotel, London U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ritz_Hotel,_London)___ , at the age of 87.

A polarising figure in British politics, Thatcher is nonetheless viewed favourably in ___E:historical rankings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_prime_ministers_of_the_United_Kingdom)___ and public opinion of British prime ministers.

Her tenure constituted a ___E:realignment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_realignment#Europe)___ towards ___E:neoliberal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoliberal)___ policies in Britain; the complex legacy attributed to this shift continues to be debated into the 21st century.
Margaret Hilda Roberts was born on 13 October 1925 in ___E:Grantham U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grantham)___ , Lincolnshire.
Her parents were ___E:Alfred Roberts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Roberts)___ (1892–1970), from Northamptonshire, and Beatrice Ethel Stephenson (1888–1960), from Lincolnshire.

Her father's maternal grandmother, Catherine Sullivan, was born in ___E:County Kerry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Kerry)___ , ___E:Ireland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland)___ .

Roberts spent her childhood in Grantham, where her father owned a ___E:tobacconist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacconist)___ 's and a grocery shop. In 1938, ___E:before the Second World War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Events_preceding_World_War_II_in_Europe)___ , the Roberts family briefly gave sanctuary to a teenage Jewish girl who had ___E:escaped Nazi Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_refugees_from_German-occupied_Europe_in_the_United_Kingdom)___ .
With her pen-friending elder sister Muriel, Margaret saved pocket money to help pay for the teenager's journey.
Alfred was an ___E:alderman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alderman)___ and a ___E:Methodist local preacher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist_local_preacher)___ .

He brought up his daughter as a strict ___E:Wesleyan Methodist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesleyan_Methodist_Church_(Great_Britain))___ ,  attending the ___E:Finkin Street Methodist Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finkin_Street_Methodist_Church)___ ,  but Margaret was more sceptical; the future scientist told a friend that she could not believe in ___E:angels U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel)___ , having calculated that they needed a ___E:breastbone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breastbone)___ 6 feet (1.8 m) long to support wings.

Alfred came from a ___E:Liberal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(UK))___ family but stood (as was then customary in local government) as an ___E:Independent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_politician)___ .

He served as Mayor of Grantham from 1945 to 1946 and lost his position as alderman in 1952 after the ___E:Labour Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK))___ won its first majority on Grantham Council in 1950.

Roberts attended ___E:Huntingtower Road Primary School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntingtower_Road_Primary_School)___ and won a scholarship to ___E:Kesteven and Grantham Girls' School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kesteven_and_Grantham_Girls%27_School)___ , a grammar school.
Her school reports showed hard work and continual improvement; her extracurricular activities included the piano, field hockey, poetry recitals, swimming and walking.

She was ___E:head girl U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_girl)___ in 1942–43,  and outside school, while the Second World War was ongoing, she voluntarily worked as a ___E:fire watcher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_watcher)___ in the local ___E:ARP service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARP_service)___ .

Other students thought of Roberts as the "star scientist", although mistaken advice regarding cleaning ink from ___E:parquetry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parquetry)___ almost caused ___E:chlorine gas poisoning U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorine_gas_poisoning)___ .

In her ___E:upper sixth year U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_form)___ , Roberts was accepted for a scholarship to study chemistry at ___E:Somerville College, Oxford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerville_College,_Oxford)___ , a women's college, starting in 1944. After another candidate withdrew, Roberts entered Oxford in October 1943.

Following her arrival at Oxford, Roberts began studies under ___E:X-ray crystallographer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_crystallographer)___ ___E:Dorothy Hodgkin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Hodgkin)___ , the tutor in chemistry for Somerville College since 1934.   Hodgkin considered Roberts a "good" student, and later recalled: "One could always rely on her producing a sensible, well-read essay."  She opted to read for a classified ___E:honours degree U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honours_degree)___ , entailing an additional year of supervised research.

As her thesis supervisor, Hodgkin assigned Roberts to work with ___E:Gerhard Schmidt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Schmidt_(crystallographer))___ , a researcher in Hodgkin's lab, to determine the structure of the antibiotic ___E:peptide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peptide)___ ___E:gramicidin S U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gramicidin_S)___ .

Although the research made some progress, the peptide's structure proved more complex than anticipated, and Schmidt would only determine its full structure much later; Roberts (by then Thatcher) learned this in the 1960s while visiting the ___E:Weizmann Institute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weizmann_Institute)___ , where her former research partner was then working.

Roberts graduated in 1947 with a ___E:second-class honours degree U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_undergraduate_degree_classification)___ in chemistry, and in 1950 also received the degree of ___E:Master of Arts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Arts_(Oxford,_Cambridge,_and_Dublin))___ (as an Oxford BA, she was entitled to the degree 21 terms after her ___E:matriculation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matriculation#United_Kingdom)___ ).

Although Hodgkin would later be critical of her former student's politics, they continued to correspond into the 1980s, and Roberts in her memoirs would describe her mentor as "ever-helpful", "a brilliant scientist and a gifted teacher".
As prime minister, she would keep a portrait of Hodgkin at ___E:10 Downing Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10_Downing_Street)___ .
Later in life, she was reportedly prouder of becoming the first prime minister with a science degree than becoming the first female prime minister.
While prime minister, she attempted to preserve Somerville as a women's college.
Twice a week outside study, she worked in a local forces canteen.
During her time at Oxford, Roberts was noted for her isolated and serious attitude.
Her first boyfriend, Tony Bray (1926–2014), recalled that she was "very thoughtful and a very good conversationalist.
That's probably what interested me. She was good at general subjects".

She was a member of ___E:Wesley Memorial Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesley_Memorial_Church)___ , became a ___E:lay preacher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lay_preacher)___ and joined the John Wesley Society.

She also attended ___E:Somerville College Chapel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerville_College_Chapel)___ and ___E:St Mary's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Church_of_St_Mary_the_Virgin)___ .
Roberts's coursework involved subjects beyond chemistry  as she was already contemplating an entry into law and politics.
Her enthusiasm for politics as a girl made Bray think of her as "unusual" and her parents as "slightly austere" and "very proper".

Roberts became President of the ___E:Oxford University Conservative Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University_Conservative_Association)___ in 1946.  She was influenced at university by political works such as ___E:Friedrich Hayek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Hayek)___ 's The Road to Serfdom (1944),  which condemned economic intervention by government as a precursor to an authoritarian state.

After graduating, Roberts secured a position as a research chemist for British Xylonite ( ___E:BX Plastics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BX_Plastics)___ ) following a series of interviews arranged by Oxford; she subsequently moved to ___E:Colchester U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colchester)___ in Essex to work at the firm.  Little is known about her brief time there.

By her own account, she was initially enthusiastic about the position, as she had been intended to function as a personal assistant to the company's head of research and development, providing opportunities to learn about ___E:operations management U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operations_management)___ : "But on my arrival it was decided that there was not enough to do in that capacity."  Instead, she seems to have researched methods of attaching ___E:polyvinyl chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyvinyl_chloride)___ (PVC) to metals.
While with the firm, she joined the ___E:Association of Scientific Workers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Scientific_Workers)___ .

In 1948, she applied for a job at ___E:Imperial Chemical Industries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Chemical_Industries)___ (ICI) but was rejected after the personnel department assessed her as "headstrong, obstinate and dangerously self-opinionated".
Jon Agar in Notes and Records argues that her understanding of modern scientific research later impacted her views as prime minister.

Roberts joined the local ___E:Conservative Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Association)___ and attended the party conference at ___E:Llandudno U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llandudno)___ , Wales, in 1948, as a representative of the University Graduate Conservative Association.

Meanwhile, she became a high-ranking affiliate of the ___E:Vermin Club U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermin_Club)___ ,   a group of grassroots Conservatives formed in response to a derogatory comment made by ___E:Aneurin Bevan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aneurin_Bevan)___ .

One of her Oxford friends was also a friend of the Chair of the ___E:Dartford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartford)___ Conservative Association in ___E:Kent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent)___ , who were looking for candidates.

Officials of the association were so impressed by her that they asked her to apply, even though she was not on the party's approved list; she was selected in January 1950 (aged 24) and added to the approved list ___E:post ante U:(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/post_ante)___ .

At a dinner following her formal adoption as Conservative candidate for Dartford in February 1949, she met divorcé ___E:Denis Thatcher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Thatcher)___ , a successful and wealthy businessman, who drove her to her Essex train.
After their first meeting, she described him to Muriel as "not a very attractive creature – very reserved but quite nice".

In preparation for the election, Roberts moved to Dartford, while she supported herself by working as a research chemist for ___E:J. Lyons and Co. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Lyons_and_Co.)___ in ___E:Hammersmith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammersmith)___ , reportedly as part of a team developing ___E:emulsifiers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emulsifier)___ for ___E:ice cream U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_cream)___ .
As the work was more theoretical in nature than during her prior role with BX Plastics, Roberts found it "more satisfying".
While at Lyons, she worked under the supervision of Hans Jellinek, who headed the company's physical chemistry section.

Jellinek assigned her to research the ___E:saponification U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saponification)___ of α-monostearin ( ___E:glycerol monostearate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glycerol_monostearate)___ ), which has properties as an emulsifier, stabiliser and food preservative.
Agar has noted the research may have been connected with the emulsification of ice cream, but only as a possibility.

In September 1951, their research was published in the Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture , a recently launched publication of the ___E:Society of Chemical Industry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Chemical_Industry)___ ,  as "The saponification of α-monostearin in a monolayer".
This would be Roberts's sole scientific publication.

In 1979, following his former assistant's election as prime minister, Jellinek, by then a professor of physical chemistry at ___E:Clarkson University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarkson_University)___ in the United States, said she had done "a very good job" on the project, "showing great determination".
She sent Jellinek a congratulatory letter upon his retirement in 1984, and another letter shortly before his death two years later.

Roberts married at ___E:Wesley's Chapel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesley%27s_Chapel)___ and her children were baptised there,  but she and her husband began attending ___E:Church of England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England)___ services and would later convert to ___E:Anglicanism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism)___ .

In the ___E:1950 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ and ___E:1951 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1951_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ general elections, Roberts was the Conservative candidate for the Labour seat of ___E:Dartford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartford_(UK_Parliament_constituency))___ .
The local party selected her as its candidate because, though not a dynamic public speaker, Roberts was well-prepared and fearless in her answers.

A prospective candidate, ___E:Bill Deedes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Deedes)___ , recalled: "Once she opened her mouth, the rest of us began to look rather second-rate."  She attracted media attention as the youngest and the only female candidate;  in 1950, she was the youngest Conservative candidate in the country.

She lost on both occasions to ___E:Norman Dodds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Dodds)___ but reduced the Labour majority by 6,000 and then a further 1,000.  During the campaigns, she was supported by her parents and by her future husband Denis Thatcher, whom she married in December 1951.   She trained at the ___E:Inns of Court School of Law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inns_of_Court_School_of_Law)___ (now part of The City Law School)  and qualified as a ___E:barrister U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barristers_in_England_and_Wales)___ in 1953 (specialising in taxation).
Denis funded his wife's studies for the ___E:bar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_association)___ .

Later that same year, their twins ___E:Carol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Thatcher)___ and ___E:Mark U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Thatcher)___ were born, delivered prematurely by Caesarean section.

In 1954, Thatcher was defeated when she sought selection to be the ___E:Conservative Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK))___ candidate for the ___E:Orpington by-election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_Orpington_by-election)___ of January 1955. She chose not to stand as a candidate in the ___E:1955 general election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ , in later years, stating: "I really just felt the twins were [...] only two, I really felt that it was too soon. I couldn't do that."  Afterwards, Thatcher began looking for a Conservative safe seat and was selected as the candidate for ___E:Finchley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finchley_(UK_Parliament_constituency))___ in April 1958 (narrowly beating ___E:Ian Montagu Fraser U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Montagu_Fraser)___ ).
She was elected as MP for the seat after a hard campaign in the ___E:1959 election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1959_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ .

Benefiting from her fortunate result in a lottery for ___E:backbenchers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backbencher)___ to propose new legislation,  Thatcher's maiden speech was, unusually, in support of her ___E:private member's bill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_member%27s_bill)___ , the ___E:Public Bodies (Admission to Meetings) Act 1960 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Bodies_(Admission_to_Meetings)_Act_1960)___ , requiring local authorities to hold their council meetings in public; the bill was successful and became law.   In 1961 she went against the Conservative Party's official position by voting for the restoration of ___E:birching U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birching)___ as a ___E:judicial corporal punishment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_corporal_punishment)___ .

Thatcher's talent and drive caused her to be mentioned as a future prime minister in her early 20s  although she herself was more pessimistic, stating as late as 1970: "There will not be a woman prime minister in my lifetime – the male population is too prejudiced."  In October 1961 she was promoted to the ___E:frontbench U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontbench)___ as ___E:Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry for Pensions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Secretary_to_the_Ministry_for_Pensions)___ by ___E:Harold Macmillan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Macmillan)___ .

Thatcher was the youngest woman in history to receive such a post, and among the first ___E:MPs elected in 1959 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_MPs_elected_in_the_1959_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ to be promoted.

After the Conservatives lost the ___E:1964 election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_United_Kingdom_general_election)___ , she became spokeswoman on housing and land. In that position, she advocated her party's policy of giving tenants the ___E:right to buy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_buy)___ their ___E:council houses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_house)___ .
